subject: anatomy
title: Vertebral canal and foraminal architecture
summary: The vertebral canal and intervertebral foramina are distinct neural corridors bounded by load-bearing bodies, pedicles, laminae and facet joints. keyPoints: The pedicle forms a lateral wall of the vertebral canal, so a medial breach can enter the canal. Pedicles connect the arch to the body and bound the canal laterally. A medial breach therefore directs the screw toward the thecal sac and its neural contents.

The disc and vertebral bodies anteriorly, and the zygapophysial joint posteriorly. The disc bulge encroaches from the anterior foraminal boundary and the facet osteophyte from posteriorly; pedicle notches form the superior and inferior boundaries.
Posterior bony roof of the canal removed; anterior vertebral body retained. The laminae form the posterior arch and canal roof. The vertebral body is the major weight-bearing component.

Posterior body displacement encroaches on the anterior canal wall and may compress the thecal contents. The posterior body surface faces the canal across the posterior longitudinal ligament and epidural tissues, so retropulsion can compromise neural structures.

subject: anatomy
title: Atlas-axis stability and head movement
summary: Upper cervical stability depends on several restraints with different roles. The transverse ligament secures the dens against the atlas, alar ligaments chiefly check rotation, and the tectorial membrane continues the posterior longitudinal ligament to the skull. Rotation and nodding can therefore be separated by movement and injury pattern.
keyPoints: Transverse ligament of the atlas. This ligament passes behind the dens between the atlas lateral masses and holds the dens against the anterior arch, resisting anterior displacement of the atlas.

Alar ligaments connecting the dens to the occipital condyles. The alar ligaments check excessive rotation. Preservation of the dens-anterior arch relationship points away from primary transverse-ligament failure.

Atlanto-axial rotation is impaired; atlanto-occipital flexion-extension is preserved. The dens is the pivot for rotation of the atlas and head. The occipital condyles move on the atlas mainly for nodding.
Tectorial membrane. The superior continuation of the posterior longitudinal ligament from C2 to the intracranial skull base is the tectorial membrane.

subject: anatomy
title: Regional vertebrae and their relationships
summary: Regional vertebral form predicts motion and adjacent structures. title: Disc mechanics and spinal ligament planes
summary: A disc distributes compression centrally while its lamellar annulus constrains movement. subject: anatomy
title: Disc location and the threatened nerve
summary: A disc level alone does not identify every threatened nerve. In the lumbar spine a lateral-recess lesion can contact a traversing root, while a foraminal lesion contacts the exiting nerve. keyPoints: L5 root. Lumbar nerves exit below their corresponding vertebrae. The L5 root descends past the L4-L5 disc toward the L5-S1 exit, whereas the L4 root is the exiting root at L4-L5.
L4 spinal nerve. The nerve exiting the L4-L5 foramen is L4. Distinguishing foraminal from traversing-root compression prevents assigning every L4-L5 lesion to L5.

C6, because C1-C7 nerves exit above their corresponding vertebrae. The C6 nerve exits above C6 through C5-C6. The extra C8 nerve exits between C7 and T1, after which nerves exit below corresponding vertebrae.

Descending cauda equina roots within the lumbar cistern. Below the normal conus, lumbar and sacral roots continue through the canal. Central compression can involve several roots, including sacral roots serving perineal and pelvic functions.

subject: anatomy
title: Roots, mixed nerves and recurrent branches
summary: Anterior and posterior roots separate efferent and afferent traffic before forming a mixed spinal nerve. Both rami then carry mixed fibers to different territories. keyPoints: The posterior root carries sensory processes, whereas the posterior ramus contains both sensory and motor fibers. A root lesion before joining can selectively interrupt sensory input. A posterior ramus lesion would also affect motor supply to intrinsic back muscles.
Posterior ramus after the spinal nerve has divided. This mixed ramus supplies intrinsic back muscles and adjacent skin. Sparing the anterior ramus accounts for preserved anterior wall function.

Motor loss may involve both ramal distributions while segmental sensory input is relatively preserved. Motor fibers leave in the anterior root and later distribute through both rami. The posterior sensory root remains intact, unlike a mixed-spinal-nerve lesion.

Recurrent meningeal (sinuvertebral) nerves re-entering the canal. These nerves return through the foramen to supply dura, ligaments, discs and blood vessels, explaining sensory access to structures inside the canal.

title: Meningeal spaces, sleeves and cord anchors
summary: Spinal dura is separated from the canal wall by a real epidural space containing fat and veins. subject: anatomy
title: Rib joints, muscle extents and arterial origins
summary: The chest wall combines posterior rib articulations, muscular and membranous intercostal layers, and arterial groups with different parent vessels. External and internal intercostal muscles have different anterior and posterior extents. External intercostals continue anteriorly as a membrane near the costal cartilages. Internal intercostals extend anteriorly to the sternum and are replaced posteriorly near the angle by an internal membrane.

subject: anatomy
title: Thoracoabdominal nerves and autonomic routes
summary: Thoracic nerves serve somatic territories and autonomic pathways that must be kept distinct. The intercostobrachial nerve accounts for medial-arm sensory loss without lower-plexus motor failure, and lower intercostal nerves continue into the abdominal wall. White and gray rami, splanchnic nerves and cardiac branches differ by destination and ganglionic stage.
keyPoints: Intercostobrachial nerve, usually the lateral cutaneous branch of T2. This thoracic sensory branch crosses the axilla to the medial upper arm. Its injury need not involve the lower brachial plexus or hand motor supply.

Anterior rami T7-T11 continue beyond the intercostal spaces into the abdominal wall. These lower thoracic anterior rami supply both thoracic and abdominal territories, so one proximal lesion can affect both.

White ramus: chiefly preganglionic route to the trunk; gray ramus: postganglionic route to the spinal nerve. This is the standard efferent sympathetic pattern. Exact branch positions and additional connections vary, so the fiber class and route are more reliable than a fixed drawing position.

Greater thoracic splanchnic nerve, containing mainly preganglionic efferents plus visceral afferents. The greater splanchnic nerve carries many fibers through the thoracic trunk without their final peripheral synapse, then passes through the crus to prevertebral ganglia. Cardiac sympathetic efferents are postganglionic.

The sympathetic fiber is postganglionic; the vagal fiber generally still synapses in cardiac ganglia near or within atrial tissues. Cardiac sympathetic fibers arise from sympathetic ganglion neurons, whereas vagal cardiac efferents are preganglionic and synapse in intrinsic cardiac ganglia.

subject: anatomy
title: Mediastinal continuity and crossing pathways
summary: Mediastinal structures change their relationships as they ascend or descend. Left gastric vein to lower esophageal venous plexuses to azygos-system drainage. The left gastric vein belongs to the portal system, while thoracic esophageal veins drain mainly through the azygos system to the SVC, creating a portosystemic connection.

Continuity of deep cervical spaces with superior and then inferior mediastinal tissue planes. The mediastinum communicates with neck spaces, including routes associated with retropharyngeal, danger, pretracheal and carotid-sheath regions. It is not sealed off at the thoracic inlet.

objectives.text: Explain different respiratory effects on caval and aortic passage from the tissue composition of their openings.
Identify the crural contribution to the esophageal antireflux barrier while distinguishing it from other diaphragmatic openings.
Distinguish median, medial and lateral arcuate structures using their underlying muscles and vessels.
Use central versus peripheral diaphragmatic sensory supply to explain different pain distributions.
Distinguish sliding from paraesophageal hiatus hernia by the position of the gastroesophageal junction.
